steps.label: Generalized linear classifiers
steps.speakerNotes: Level: undergraduate (year 3). Made from the lecture lec05-kp13 with view-from-text-v3: pages were planned first and each page is mainly one native infographic (designed in HTML and converted to native nodes), with the terms defined on the same page. 9 pages; every number is computed by program.

steps.label: Sandwiched classes
steps.speakerNotes: This is the first page of KP13. Prerequisites: the linear discriminant function (KP01 to KP03), the squared error (KP06) and matrix multiplication with transpose. The one-dimensional example is my own design: class A at x equal to minus 3, minus 2, 2, 3 and class B at minus 1, 0, 1, 7 points in all. A program tries every threshold and direction and at most 5 are right: with the threshold at 1.5, the three B points and the A points at 2 and 3 are right, while the A points at minus 3 and minus 2 are wrong. The reason is that A lies on both sides of B, so the size of x alone cannot say on both sides (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the new coordinates (x, x²).

steps.label: New coordinates
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the sandwiched classes. This page changes coordinates. A feature mapping uses a set of functions fi to replace x by new coordinates y equal to (f1(x), …, fk(x)). Here take y equal to (x, x squared) and compute point by point: A at x equal to minus 3, minus 2, 2, 3 gives x squared equal to 9, 4, 4, 9; B at minus 1, 0, 1 gives 1, 0, 1. Every A has y2 at least 4 and every B at most 1, so the horizontal line y2 equal to 2.5 separates the two classes, which is a linear classifier in the new coordinates (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the bend seen back in x.

steps.label: Back in x
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the new coordinates (x, x²). This page looks back in x. A generalized linear classifier lifts with fixed nonlinear functions fi and then designs an ordinary linear classifier; linear means linear in the weights wi. Step by step for this example: take f1 equal to x and f2 equal to x squared; the horizontal line y2 equal to 2.5 corresponds to w0 equal to minus 2.5, w1 equal to 0 and w2 equal to 1; so g(x) equals minus 2.5 plus x squared, with g above 0 called A and below 0 called B; g equal to 0 gives x equal to plus or minus the square root of 2.5, about plus or minus 1.58, with A outside and B inside. One line in the new space is two points in the original space, that is, the boundary bends along the x axis (computed by program). Next, the next page covers XOR once more.

steps.label: XOR once more
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the bend seen back in x. This page looks at XOR again with the same idea. The four points are (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1), and a class means the two coordinates differ, that is, (0,1) and (1,0) are A. Add the coordinate y3 equal to x1 times x2; take g equal to x1 plus x2 minus 2 y3 minus 0.5 and substitute point by point: (0,0) gives minus 0.5, (0,1) gives plus 0.5, (1,0) gives plus 0.5 and (1,1) gives minus 0.5, so one plane separates the four points. KP02 combined two lines; here it is one fixed mapping plus one plane (computed by program). Next, the next page covers how the weights are computed.

steps.label: Computing weights
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on XOR once more. This page computes the weights. The normal equation is the solution that minimizes the squared error between Φ w and the target t: w equals the inverse of (Φ transpose Φ) times Φ transpose t. Each row of Φ is (1, f1, …, fk) of one sample, here (1, x, x squared); in t, A is plus 1 and B is minus 1. The seven points of section 1 give w equal to (minus 0.810, 0, 0.238); the seven g values are 1.333, 0.143, 0.143, 1.333, minus 0.571, minus 0.810, minus 0.571, whose signs all match the targets, so all seven are right (computed by program). It differs from the hand-set (minus 2.5, 0, 1) of page 3; both classify everything right, and least squares aims at the smallest squared error, not at the largest distance of the boundary. Next, the next page covers the concentric rings.

steps.label: Concentric rings
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on how the weights are computed. This page moves to two-dimensional concentric rings and uses a program. The setup is my own design and reproducible: 100 points per class, the angle uniform over 0 to 2π, the radius normal with mean 1.0 and standard deviation 0.15 for A and mean 2.2 and standard deviation 0.2 for B, random seed 0; targets are plus 1 for A and minus 1 for B, and both feature sets use least squares. The linear features [1, x1, x2], 3 of them, get 102 right, 51%, which is guessing; the quadratic features, 6 of them, get 199 right, 99.5%. For the quadratic features g equal to 0 is a circle of radius about 1.71 in the original space, between the two rings, whose mean radii are about 0.98 and 2.19. This is accuracy on the same training data, so it only shows what can be represented, not generalization. The number of quadratic features is l times l plus 3 over 2: 5, 65, 5150 for l equal to 2, 10, 100 (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the multi-class case.

steps.label: Multi-class
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the concentric rings. This page handles several classes: M classes need M weight vectors, and the class with the largest wr transpose y plus wr0 is chosen. The example is my own design: nine points in one dimension, with x equal to minus 3, minus 2.5, minus 2 in class 1, minus 0.5, 0, 0.5 in class 2 and 2, 2.5, 3 in class 3. The targets are one-hot, that is, the target vector of class r has only its r-th entry equal to 1; with features (1, x, x squared) least squares solves three weight sets and all nine are right. With only (1, x) just 7 are right, and the middle class keeps only x equal to 0, where the three g tie at 1/3 and the middle class is taken (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the comparison with projection pursuit.

steps.label: Projection pursuit
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the multi-class case. This page compares projection pursuit: g(x) is the sum of fi of wi transpose x; the argument of fi is the projection of x on the direction wi, and the directions and functions are optimized together. In the doubling test, doubling w exactly doubles g for the generalized linear classifier; for projection pursuit (f a sigmoid, input 1, w equal to 1) f(2) equals 0.881, not 2 f(1) equal to 1.462, so it is not linear in w and needs two-stage alternating optimization. If fi is fixed in advance as a sigmoid, it is a one-hidden-layer neural network, which multilayer perceptrons have replaced in practice. To remember: generalized linear is a fixed mapping plus a learnable linear layer; a multilayer perceptron is a learnable mapping plus a learnable linear layer (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the exercises.

steps.label: Exercises
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the comparison with projection pursuit. Two exercises with features y equal to (x1 squared, x2 squared) and g equal to y1 plus y2 minus 4, where g above 0 is A. Q1: which class are (1,1), (3,0), (0, minus 2.5)? For (1,1): 1 plus 1 minus 4 equals minus 2, class B; for (3,0): 9 plus 0 minus 4 equals 5, class A; for (0, minus 2.5): 0 plus 6.25 minus 4 equals 2.25, class A. Q2: what shape is g equal to 0 in the x plane? g equal to 0 means x1 squared plus x2 squared equal to 4, a circle of radius 2: a straight line in y space and bent in x space (computed by program). That ends this unit; next, move on to the next unit.
